title: RBI Swap Facility Draws $20.7 Billion in Forex Inflows as FCNR Deposits Surge
excerpt: The central bank's concessional swap window has attracted $17.4 billion in FCNR(B) deposits alone since June, though early mobilisation trails initial market estimates of $50-70 billion.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • RBI's swap facility attracted $20.72 billion in forex inflows by July 17, 2026.
  • FCNR(B) deposits made up $17.4 billion of the total inflows.
  • Banks are offering NRIs interest rates of 5.5-7.1%, significantly higher than before.
  • Early mobilisation of $3-6 billion is below initial estimates of $50-70 billion.
  • Most demand is from NRIs in Gulf countries, attracted by favorable tax treatment.

  • RBI's concessional swap facility has attracted USD 20.72 billion in total forex inflows as of July 17, 2026, with FCNR(B) deposits accounting for USD 17.4 billion.
  • Overseas Foreign Currency Borrowings (OFCBs) contributed USD 1.97 billion and External Commercial Borrowings (ECBs) added USD 1.34 billion to the total.
  • Banks are offering NRIs 5.5-7.1% on dollar deposits — up from 3.5-4% before the scheme — by passing on savings from RBI absorbing the full hedging cost.
  • Despite the strong start, early mobilisation of $3-6 billion by individual banks trails initial market estimates of $50-70 billion, with the September 30 deadline looming.

RBI Reports Strong Early Numbers

The Reserve Bank of India on Monday disclosed that its concessional swap facility, introduced in early June to bolster foreign currency inflows, has attracted USD 20.72 billion in aggregate since its launch. The data, covering flows through July 17, marks the first official progress update on a scheme that has been the subject of intense market speculation since it was announced on June 5.

Of the total, Foreign Currency Non-Resident (Bank) deposits — the centrepiece of the facility — accounted for USD 17.406 billion, according to the RBI's statement. Overseas Foreign Currency Borrowings by authorised dealer banks contributed USD 1.97 billion, while External Commercial Borrowings by public sector undertakings added USD 1.342 billion.

"With a view to strengthening our balance of payments and incentivising capital inflows, the RBI had announced a series of measures, including a facility for offering concessional swaps for fresh FCNR(B) deposits, OFCB and ECB inflows on June 5, 2026," the central bank said.

How the Zero-Cost Swap Works

The scheme's design addresses a longstanding friction in NRI deposit mobilisation. Ordinarily, when a bank collects dollar deposits, it faces a hedging cost of roughly 2.5-3% to convert those dollars into rupees for domestic lending while guaranteeing repayment in the original currency. That cost capped the interest rates banks could offer on FCNR(B) deposits, typically leaving them at 3.5-4% — barely competitive against US Treasury yields.

Under the new facility, the RBI absorbs the entire hedging cost through an at-par swap. Banks sell dollars to the central bank today and agree to buy them back at the same exchange rate at maturity, with no premium. The zero-cost hedge has allowed banks to push deposit rates sharply higher.

"This lets banks offer 6.5%, which is likely to attract more deposits."</p><cite>— Gaura Sengupta, Chief Economist, IDFC First Bank</cite></blockquote> <p>Several banks have responded aggressively."

"This lets banks offer 6.5%, which is likely to attract more deposits."</p><cite>— Gaura Sengupta, Chief Economist, IDFC First Bank</cite></blockquote> <p>Several banks have responded aggressively."

"Unlike the 2024 framework, the RBI is now absorbing the full 3.5% interest rate cost. This lets banks offer 6.5%, which is likely to attract more deposits."

— Gaura Sengupta, Chief Economist, IDFC First Bank

Several banks have responded aggressively. YES Bank and AU Small Finance Bank are offering 7.10% on five-year USD deposits, up roughly 310 basis points from prior rates, according to publicly available data. HDFC Bank has raised its rate to 6% across USD maturities, while Central Bank of India has moved to 6% from approximately 2.5%. Deposits under the scheme are also exempt from CRR and SLR requirements, improving the economics further for banks.

Mobilisation Trails Estimates, But Banks Are Optimistic

The USD 20.72 billion headline figure, while substantial, sits well below the $50-70 billion market estimates that circulated immediately after the scheme's launch, according to The Hindu BusinessLine. Nearly six weeks into the programme, individual banks have collectively mobilised roughly $3-6 billion, prompting a more measured outlook across the industry.

Among public sector banks, Punjab National Bank has been the most bullish, with Managing Director and CEO Ashok Chandra projecting FCNR(B) deposits of $2.5 billion by September, up from $425 million currently. Union Bank of India is targeting $1.5-2 billion, while Indian Bank — which has already collected $140 million — is aiming for $2 billion and reports a visible pipeline of nearly $1 billion. South Indian Bank is targeting $1 billion, and Central Bank of India has set a goal of $400 million.

Major private lenders, including HDFC Bank, ICICI Bank, Kotak Mahindra Bank, Federal Bank and YES Bank, have not disclosed mobilisation numbers, preferring to review progress at the end of the September quarter.

ICICI Bank has flagged that FCNR(B) deposits could mildly dilute net interest margins because of the higher rates being offered. Federal Bank, meanwhile, sees strong potential among NRIs in the Middle East, Singapore and Hong Kong and plans to offer leverage of 8-12 times against deposits.

Why NRIs in the Gulf Are Leading Demand

Most incremental inflows are coming from retail NRIs in Gulf countries, particularly the UAE, along with pockets of demand from Singapore and Hong Kong. These jurisdictions offer favourable tax treatment on overseas deposit income, making the 6-7% rates on FCNR(B) deposits especially attractive against US Treasury yields of 4-4.2%.

Demand from the United States and Australia has been relatively muted. NRIs in those markets have access to competing fixed-income alternatives, including certificates of deposit at US banks offering 3.5-4% for short promotional tenures. Additionally, tax liabilities in the country of residence, FEMA compliance requirements and broader portfolio considerations all influence participation, according to bankers and advisers.

The narrowing India-US yield differential — now approximately 200-220 basis points compared with 650-800 basis points in 2013 — has also reduced the carry advantage, limiting the scheme's pull relative to its predecessor.

Echoes of 2013, But Different Economics

The current scheme draws direct comparisons to the FCNR(B) swap window launched under then-RBI Governor Raghuram Rajan in 2013, which brought in nearly $34 billion — $26 billion through FCNR(B) deposits and $8 billion through ECBs. That facility accounted for roughly 12% of India's forex reserves at the time.

But the economics have shifted. Brokerage MUFG has noted that higher US interest rates and lower Indian bond yields have compressed the rate differential, making it harder to replicate the 2013 outcome through deposits alone. Nomura, however, estimates the combined package — including FCNR(B), ECB incentives, tax exemptions on government bonds for FPIs, and equity market reforms — could attract up to $55 billion, with the bulk expected in August and September as bank marketing campaigns intensify and NRI awareness grows.

The facility for FCNR(B) deposits runs until September 30, while the swap window remains open until October 16. The ECB and OFCB components have longer deadlines, with borrowings eligible through December 31, 2026, and the swap window open until January 15, 2027.

What It Means for the Diaspora

For NRIs weighing the opportunity, the calculus has shifted materially. FCNR(B) rates of 6-7.1% on three-to-five-year dollar deposits, with no currency risk and interest that is tax-free in India, represent a historically unusual window. With leverage of 8-12 times available from Indian banks — and up to 19 times from some overseas institutions — the effective returns can amplify further, though with proportionally higher risk.

The deposits carry a mandatory one-year lock-in, with premature withdrawal permitted thereafter at the bank's discretion. Principal and interest are fully repatriable. The minimum deposit size starts at $500-1,000, though the higher rates and leverage options are primarily targeting high-net-worth NRIs with larger balances.

With roughly 10 weeks remaining until the September 30 deadline, the pace of mobilisation will determine whether the scheme approaches its ambitious targets — or settles into a solid but more modest contribution to India's external sector defence.
